citation: Data from Comparitech Ransomware Intelligence Platform (ransomware.comparitech.com)

corpus.what_is_included: Every ransomware attack claim drawn from the source spreadsheets that survives ingest becomes one incident with a source ledger and an evidence grade, whether or not this platform can independently confirm it, confirmation_status distinguishes the two; see the confirmation rule below. See /data/status/latest.json for current corpus figures.
corpus.what_is_excluded: A source row is excluded, never silently dropped, for one of a small, named set of reasons: no organisation name or usable content, an organisation named but no source link of any kind, a date cell that could not be parsed as a month, a country cell that did not resolve to an ISO 3166-1 country, or, the one reason withheld by name rather than merely by row: A leak-site claim with no retained source of any kind. Withheld by default, see the platform's withholding policy. Every excluded row is counted, by reason, at /data/exclusions/index.json; see this document's withholding policy above for which reasons are named there and which are not.
corpus.date_precision: Month precision (YYYY-MM) throughout. A cited source may report the specific day an attack occurred or was disclosed; this platform does not retain or publish it, see this document's limitations.

source_classes.label: Attacker stated
source_classes.definition: The only source is the ransomware group's own leak-site listing or extortion statement, with nothing independent behind it. An attack is never confirmed on this alone.

source_classes.label: Defacement observed
source_classes.definition: The ransomware group claimed the attack AND Comparitech researchers saw the hackers' own message left on the affected organisation's website. The claim is the attacker's; the corroboration is ours and first-hand, which is why this confirms an attack where a leak-site listing alone does not. It carries the same weight as an attacker statement because it is still the weakest evidence we publish. These cases are rare.

source_classes.label: Comparitech editorial
source_classes.definition: Comparitech's own reporting. Carries the same weight as third_party_reported, because it is real reporting, but it is excluded entirely from the independence term and from the confirmation rule below: grading our own article as independent corroboration of our own dataset would be circular, one level worse than the ordinary publisher-independence problem it would otherwise resemble.

source_classes.label: Data breach notification
source_classes.definition: The victim has issued a data breach notification, confirming a cybersecurity incident at a time when a hacker has claimed an attack. The report may not mention ransomware specifically, but the incident details and date match up to the hackers' claim.

source_classes.label: Third-party reported
source_classes.definition: An independent news outlet or research organisation reported the incident.

source_classes.label: Victim confirmed
source_classes.definition: The named organisation itself has acknowledged the incident through a press release, a regulatory filing, or a statement to a reporter attributed to the organisation.

confirmation.rule: An incident is confirmed when at least one of its sources is neither attacker_stated nor editorial, i.e. at least one source class carries verification independent of both the attacker's own claim and this platform's own reporting of that claim. attacker_stated and editorial sources may both be present on a confirmed incident; neither one, alone or together, is sufficient to confirm it.
confirmation.enforced_by: A database trigger on the incidents table, evaluated at write time. Application code reads confirmation_status; it is never assigned directly by an editor or an ingest script. This platform's grading module mirrors the same rule in code for admin-preview purposes, and a database test asserts the two agree for every source class, including editorial, the trigger remains the sole authority.

grade.formula: grade = the weight of the incident's confirmation type. There is no sum: the scale has exactly four values. Victim confirmation 10.0; breach notification filed by the victim 7.5; third-party report 5.0; attacker statement 2.5. ⛔ TWO TERMS WERE REMOVED ON 2026-10-02 AND NEITHER IS COMING BACK AS A HIDDEN ZERO. An INDEPENDENCE bonus (+1.0 for a second distinct publisher, +1.5 for a third) was dropped because on this corpus an additional source is usually either a later disclosure or a second outlet working from the same leak-site post, it measured how newsworthy the victim was, not how well evidenced the attack was, and a larger victim scored higher for being larger. THREE COMPLETENESS bonuses (+0.5 each for a town-level location, a named group and a disclosed impact figure) were dropped because a fact that was never disclosed is not weak evidence, it is an absent fact, and charging an incident for it conflated how much is KNOWN with how well it is CONFIRMED. A second source therefore does not raise a grade, and an undisclosed ransom figure does not lower one.
grade.source_strength: The weight of the single strongest source class present, never a sum or an average across sources. One regulator filing outweighs any number of leak-site mentions; ten weak sources do not add up to one strong one.
grade.confirmation: The grade IS the confirmation type's weight: victim confirmation 10.0, breach notification filed by the victim 7.5, third-party report 5.0, attacker statement 2.5, defacement we saw on the victim's own site 2.5. ⛔ THE TYPE IS THE EDITOR'S, AND IT OUTRANKS THE SOURCES WE HOLD. Where our editor has recorded a stated confirmation type for an incident, that type sets the grade, even where the links in that incident's ledger classify lower. Her ruling, and the reason is that a URL does not reveal what she read inside it: a third-party report frequently quotes a victim statement in full, and the ledger can only see that the publisher was a third party. Where she has recorded no type, the grade falls back to the strongest class in the ledger. ⛔ BOTH NUMBERS ARE PUBLISHED SO A READER CAN SEE THE DISAGREEMENT RATHER THAN TAKE OUR WORD FOR IT: `evidence_grade` and `confirmation_level` carry the editor's type, while `strongest_source_class` on the same incident carries what its links alone support. They differ for a substantial minority of the corpus, by design, and /evidence publishes the two distributions side by side. ⛔ A VICTIM'S OWN STATEMENT OUTRANKS THEIR BREACH NOTIFICATION, which reverses the order this document published before 2026-10-02. The sources classed as regulator filings are almost entirely state attorney-general and federal portals hosting the VICTIM's own notification, and such a notification frequently confirms a 'cybersecurity incident' without ever using the word ransomware. For a ransomware dataset that is the weaker claim, however official the letterhead. ⛔ COMPARITECH'S OWN REPORTING (source class editorial) IS NOT A LEVEL. Where it is the only source the incident is graded as a victim confirmation, because we are the sole source when the affected organisation gave us a statement directly. Where it sits beside another outlet's reporting it is a citation and does not raise the level, because we must not corroborate ourselves. ⛔ DISTINCT PUBLISHERS ARE STILL PUBLISHED PER INCIDENT and no longer scored. The reduction to a registrable domain uses a short allow-list of multi-part public suffixes rather than a full public-suffix list, so some genuinely distinct outlets merge into one entry; `sources[].publisher_domain` on each incident is unreduced, so a reader can check. ⛔ WHILE DATA_UNCONFIRMED_PUBLIC IS SHUT NO PUBLISHED GRADE CAN FALL BELOW 2.5, and that is unreachable by construction rather than merely unoccupied, so a reader who sees nothing below it is seeing a consequence of the scale and not a gap in the corpus: every type that satisfies the confirmation rule weighs at least 2.5, and an incident satisfying none of them is withheld. ⛔ THE LOWEST BAND IS NOT EMPTY, AND WHAT SITS IN IT IS NOT AN ATTACKER'S WORD. Two types share the weight 2.5 and only one of them confirms: a bare attacker statement does not, and a defacement we saw on the victim's own site does, because the corroboration is first-hand and ours. So a published incident at the floor is always the latter. ⛔ DO NOT READ A COUNT IN THAT BAND AS ATTACKER-ONLY EVIDENCE - read it as the rarest thing we publish, an attack we confirmed by looking at the victim's website ourselves. ⛔ ONCE THE FLAG IS OPEN THE FLOOR IS FULLY OCCUPIED, and that is the clearest statement of what the flag does: every withheld incident sits at the floor exactly because an attacker's claim is the only thing asserting it. No count is given here for either state, because a count in this document is a cached claim of ours that the live feed can contradict; /data/incidents/index.json publishes the grade distribution, and /data/status/latest.json the withheld total.

provenance_classes.definition: Taken directly from a cited source: the organisation name, the occurrence date, and any impact figure a source itself states.
provenance_classes.applies_to: Organisation name, occurrence month, source class, publisher domain, and any impact figure a cited source itself reports.

provenance_classes.definition: Applied by a human editor at ingest time, rather than lifted verbatim from one citation. Not sourced from a single article, and not produced by any automated process.
provenance_classes.applies_to: Sector classification, geocode precision placement, and group alias resolution. Alias resolution is recorded per record, where a source happened to use an alternate group name, it is not a corpus-wide reconciliation pass, and no alias is published for most groups.

provenance_classes.definition: Forwarded from the victim's or the attacker's own statement, without independent audit. This platform republishes the figure; it does not verify it.
provenance_classes.applies_to: Every quantified impact figure this platform publishes, records affected, data stolen, and ransom demanded, is the victim's or the attacker's own claim, carried through as declared, never independently measured.

provenance_classes.definition: A value this platform itself computed by running an automated test or measurement process, independent of any source's own claim.
provenance_classes.applies_to: Nothing in this dataset today. No field on this platform is produced by an automated measurement process, every classification is sourced or editorial, and every quantified figure is declared. Named here so this vocabulary is complete rather than acquiring a class only after one is needed.

provenance_classes.definition: Computed from one or more of the classes above, or from another derived value, a count, a sum, a grade, a breadth figure, a generated identifier. Makes no claim about the world on its own; it is arithmetic over claims already made.
provenance_classes.applies_to: Every published count, sum, grade and breadth figure, plus every derived identifier (a data_url, an ETag input), most numbers and pointers on this platform, since almost nothing published is a raw pass-through of a single source field.

withholding.policy: This platform withholds one category of INCIDENT by default: an unconfirmed incident, one whose every cited source is a class that cannot confirm it on its own (attacker_stated; the same classes confirmation.rule above excludes). The count of withheld incidents is published at /data/status/latest.json's corpus.unconfirmed; the organisation each one names, and its own incident document, are withheld while it stays unconfirmed. ⛔ THIS IS A DIFFERENT POPULATION FROM /data/exclusions/index.json's `withheld` total: that feed counts SOURCE ROWS dropped at ingest for carrying no retained source of any kind, rows that never became an incident in this corpus at all, and are not counted in corpus.unconfirmed. Never add the two figures together, and never treat one as a subset or a restatement of the other. Every other exclusion reason (a blank row, a row with no source link, an unparseable date, an unresolvable country) is ordinary ingest housekeeping, names nobody as an attack victim, and is never withheld. The single predicate that decides which incidents are withheld is implemented once, in this platform's own code; this document names the policy it enforces, not a second copy of it.

flags.name: DATA_UNCONFIRMED_PUBLIC
flags.opens: The unconfirmed incident corpus and its per-incident documents, every incident withheld under the policy above, plus removes the withheld split from /data/exclusions/index.json's reason ledger. Additive only: setting it never removes anything a reader could already see while it was unset.
flags.default: Unset, the unconfirmed corpus is withheld until an operator explicitly opens it.

refresh.what_runs: Ingest (scripts/ingest.ts) reads the source spreadsheets and writes the corpus, operator-invoked, not scheduled. A separate nightly job (scripts/recompute.ts, 03:00 UTC) regrades every incident with the same formula published above and refreshes this platform's aggregate views; it never re-ingests a source and never touches a locked snapshot. The "daily" cadence this registry declares for every /data feed describes how often published data is expected to move, not a claim that every step above runs on an automated timer.

limitations: Every source's link_status is 'unchecked' today, no link-checking job has run yet, so a source cited here may since have moved or gone dead without this platform knowing.

No source is archived, archived_url and archived_sha256 are null on every citation in the corpus; there is no archive capture pipeline yet. The bytes themselves would never be served even once one exists, see /data/evidence/<slug>.json's archive_policy for why.
Every incident date is month precision (YYYY-MM), never day. A cited source may report the specific day an attack occurred or was disclosed; this platform does not retain or publish it.

Source coverage skews English-language. Ingest draws from English-language news coverage and regulator filings; an incident reported only in a non-English outlet is less likely to be retained, or to reach a stronger source class, independent of how significant the incident actually was.

Every quantified impact figure (records affected, data stolen, ransom demanded) is declared, not audited, see provenance_classes' 'declared' entry. This platform forwards the victim's or the attacker's own claim; it does not independently verify it.

Independence (see grade.independence) under-counts corroboration for outlets under an unlisted multi-part public suffix: the registrable-domain reduction uses a short, hand-maintained suffix list, and a hostname it does not recognise collapses to the bare suffix instead of its true publisher, merging genuinely distinct outlets into one entry. This always under-counts independence; it never over-counts. No corpus-wide figure is published here, two independent measurements of its extent disagreed, so neither is safe to publish. A reader can check any one incident directly: /data/evidence/<slug>.json publishes derivation.independence.publishers (the reduced set) alongside sources[].publisher_domain (unreduced, as retrieved), so the collapse is visible without trusting this platform's own arithmetic.

Group alias resolution (provenance class 'editorial') is recorded only where ingest happened to capture an alternate name a source used for a group, it is not a corpus-wide reconciliation pass, and no alias is published for most groups. Where a resolution is absent, two records naming what is genuinely the same group under different names may be under-merged (counted as two groups instead of one); this platform never over-merges two genuinely distinct groups into one.
